rationale: Extensive literature evaluation reveals that human disease associated with KLHL20 (OMIM #621390) is exclusively established as an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous de novo missense variants, primarily a recurrent hotspot variant (c.1069G>A, p.Gly357Arg in 11 of 14 reported individuals) clustering in the Kelch-type beta-propeller domain. No biallelic loss-of-function variants or autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental syndromes have been established or characterized in clinical cohorts for KLHL20. Furthermore, microcephaly and structural brain malformations are absent as core or defining features in the delineated cohort. Therefore, the hypothesis asserting that biallelic loss-of-function variants cause an expanded autosomal recessive syndrome with microcephaly or structural brain malformations is unsupported and contradicted by the established dominant missense-specific mechanism.

evidence.text: Sleyp et al. delineated the clinical and molecular spectrum of KLHL20-related neurodevelopmental disorder across 14 patients, all of whom carried de novo heterozygous missense variants, with 11 harboring the recurrent p.Gly357Arg variant. Phenotypes were characterized by mild to severe intellectual disability, febrile seizures or epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, and subtle facial dysmorphisms, without recessive inheritance or documented structural brain malformations.

source.title: De novo missense variants in the E3 ubiquitin ligase adaptor KLHL20 cause a developmental disorder with intellectual disability, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder
source.quote: We studied 14 patients with de novo missense variants in KLHL20, delineating a genetic syndrome with patients having mild to severe intellectual disability, febrile seizures or epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, and subtle dysmorphic facial features. We observed a recurrent de novo missense variant in 11 patients (NM_014458.4:c.1069G>A p.[Gly357Arg]).

source.quote: KLHL20 was first reported in relation to autosomal dominant (AD) neurodevelopmental disorder in 2022 (Sleyp et al., PMID: 36214804). Phenotypic features in individuals with heterozygous KLHL20 variants include mild to severe intellectual disability, febrile seizures or epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, and subtle dysmorphic facial features.

evidence.text: Systematic reviews of cullin-RING ligase substrate receptors identify KLHL20 specifically among substrate adaptors where dominant heterozygous missense variants in the Kelch domain alter substrate recognition, contrasting with standard loss-of-function or recessive degradation models.

source.title: Cullin–RING receptors in rare disease biology
source.quote: KLHL20 missense variants likely define a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring growth or developmental delays and epilepsy, acting through modified substrate recognition surfaces.

conflicts: No conflicting clinical cohorts exist; all published cohorts describe dominant de novo missense variants clustering in the Kelch-type beta-propeller domain rather than biallelic loss-of-function variants.

new_directions.question_text: Do complete loss-of-function homozygous mutations in Klhl20 result in embryonic lethality in mammalian model organisms, explaining their absence in living human clinical cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Assessing knockout Klhl20 viability in mouse models would clarify whether complete loss-of-function is incompatible with life, explaining the restriction of human disease to heterozygous missense variants.

new_directions.question_text: Does the recurrent p.Gly357Arg variant act via a dominant-negative interference or a toxic gain-of-function degron mechanism rather than simple haploinsufficiency?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the molecular pathomechanism within the CUL3-KLHL20 complex will determine whether loss-of-function vs dominant toxic properties dictate disease severity.
